'''''Leucaena''''' is a genus of [[flowering plant]]s in the [[Mimosoideae|mimosoid clade]] of the subfamily [[Caesalpinioideae]] of the family [[Fabaceae]]. It contains about 24 species of [[tree]]s and [[shrub]]s, which are commonly known as '''leadtrees'''.<ref name="ITIS">{{ITIS |id=26764 |taxon=''Leucaena'' |accessdate=23 March 2010}}</ref> They are native to the [[Americas]], ranging from [[Texas]] in the [[United States]] south to [[Peru]].<ref name="Plant-Book">{{cite book |url=https://archive.org/details/plantbookportabl00mabb |url-access=registration |first=D.J. |last=Mabberley |year=1997 |title=The Plant-Book: A portable dictionary of the vascular plants |edition=2nd |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge, England |isbn=978-0-521-41421-0 |page=[https://archive.org/details/plantbookportabl00mabb/page/n425 406]}}</ref> The generic name is derived from the [[Greek language|Greek]] word λευκός (''leukos''), meaning "white", referring to the [[flower]]s.<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eMgaXGsBEWIC |title=Sappi What's in a Name? |first=Hugh |last=Glen |year=2004 |publisher=Jacana Media  |isbn=978-1-77009-040-8 |page=39}}</ref>

==Uses==
''Leucaena'' species are grown for their variety of uses, including as [[green manure]], a [[charcoal]] source, [[livestock]] [[fodder]], and for [[soil conservation]]. The seeds (jumbie beans) can be used as beads. ''Leucaena'' planted for [[firewood]] on an area of {{convert|120|km2|sqmi|abbr=on}} will yield an energy equivalent of 1 million [[Barrel of oil equivalent|barrels of oil]] per year. [[Anthelmintic]] [[Medicinal plant|medicines]] are made from extracts of ''Leucaena'' seeds in [[Sumatra]], [[Indonesia]].<ref name="Plant-Book"/>

Some species (namely ''[[Leucaena leucocephala]]'') have edible [[fruit]]s (as unripe) and [[seed]]s. The seeds of ''[[Leucaena esculenta]]'' (in Mexico called ''guaje'' or ''huaje'') are eaten with [[salt]] in [[Mexico]]. In other species high levels of [[mimosine]] may lead to [[Alopecia|hair loss]] and [[infertility]] in non-[[ruminant]]s.<ref name="Plant-Book"/>
